dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: How are you, Lina?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Good, and you?

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: I'm a little tired today.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Why? What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: I didn't sleep well yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Poor thing, have a coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: That's what I'll do, thanks.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: And I'm happy because tomorrow is a day off.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Yeah, true, I forgot.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Don't forget, and rest a little.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: OK, bless you.

lessons.culture: In Lebanon "كيفك؟" is a greeting more than a real question, and the usual answer is "منيح، الحمد لله" whatever the mood; a close friend will follow up with "شو فيك؟" if you look off. Saying "زعلان" or "تعبان" plainly is normal mainly with family and close friends.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: 'كيفك اليوم؟'. Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but bookish; "الحمد لله" is the natural spoken answer here.

exercises.tip: "الحمد لله" is added almost automatically after saying you're fine.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: 'شو فيك، شكلك تعبان؟'. Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: That is formal written Arabic, not how tiredness is admitted in conversation.

exercises.tip: "شوي" softens the admission, like saying "a little".

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'أنا ___ كتير، بدي آكل شي.' Meaning: I'm very hungry, I want to eat something.

too_formal.feedback: Formal way of stating hunger; "جوعان" is the word actually used.

exercises.tip: "جوعان/جوعانة" changes with the speaker's gender.

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'أنا ___ من هالشي.' Meaning: I'm scared of this.

too_formal.feedback: Formal spelling and register; "خايف" is how it's said out loud.

exercises.tip: "خايف" for a man, "خايفة" for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Translate: 'I'm very happy today.'

too_formal.feedback: "سعيد" is the formal word for happy; Lebanese say "مبسوط".

exercises.tip: "مبسوط" is by far the everyday word for happy, not "سعيد".

exercises.prompt: Translate: 'I'm a little worried about the exam.'

too_formal.item: أنا قلق بعض الشيء بخصوص الامتحان
too_formal.feedback: Overly formal phrasing for a simple everyday worry.

exercises.tip: "عالامتحان" is the fast, run-together way of saying "على الامتحان".

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I'm worried'?

too_formal.feedback: Nobody speaks like this out loud; it belongs in writing, not conversation.

exercises.tip: "قلقان" comes from the same root as "قلق", worry.

exercises.prompt: "زعلان" means:

too_formal.feedback: That is a dictionary-style gloss, not the plain answer expected here.

exercises.tip: "زعلان" is milder than "angry"; closer to "upset" or "put out".

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: 'كتير / اليوم / مبسوط / أنا'.

too_formal.feedback: Formal register and word order, not the conversational sentence being practised.

exercises.tip: The subject "أنا" comes first, then the feeling, then how much, then when.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: 'من / خايف / هالشي / أنا'.

too_formal.feedback: Formal spelling "خائف" and "هذا الأمر" instead of the spoken forms.

exercises.tip: "هالشي" is the everyday contraction of "هذا الشي".

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.transliteration: shu ra2yak nrou7 3al ma6ma3 el jdiid?
dialogue.english: What do you think, shall we go to the new restaurant?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.english: Maybe, but it's very expensive.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: لأ، مش هيك، سمعت إنو الأسعار منيحة
dialogue.transliteration: la2, mish heek, sme3et 2inno el as3aar mnii7a
dialogue.english: No, it's not like that, I heard the prices are good.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.english: Who told you that?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: My friend, and in my opinion he knows.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.english: I don't agree with you, he always exaggerates.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: True, you're a bit right.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.english: Let's see the menu first.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Exactly, that's better.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.english: And if it's good we'll go, agreed?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: OK, that works.

pair.english: What do you think of this idea?

response.english: No, I don't agree with you.

pair.transliteration: hayda esh shi ghalat, mish heek?

lessons.culture: In Lebanon people usually soften a disagreement with "يمكن" or "بس" before saying no outright, and "معك حق" is offered generously to keep the conversation friendly. Lively arguing over an opinion between friends is normal and rarely meant as an insult.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: 'شو رأيك بهالفكرة؟'. Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but written-style; "برأيي منيحة" is what is said aloud.

exercises.tip: "منيح/منيحة" is the everyday word for good.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: 'بتوافقني؟'. Give a natural reply saying no.

too_formal.feedback: "كلا" and the full formal sentence sound like a speech, not a chat.

exercises.tip: Lebanese say "لأ" with a glottal stop at the end for no.

exercises.prompt: Complete: '___ حق، هيك أحسن.' Meaning: You're right, this is better. (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: "أنت محق" is correct but formal; "معك حق" is what people say.

exercises.tip: "معك" is for a man, "معِك" for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Complete: '___، خليني فكر شوي.' Meaning: Maybe, let me think a little.

too_formal.feedback: "ربما" is formal; "يمكن" is the spoken maybe.

exercises.tip: "يمكن" opens a softened answer, and "بس" then brings the objection.

exercises.prompt: Translate: 'I don't agree with you.'

too_formal.feedback: Formal written phrasing; the spoken form uses "ما بـ" on the verb.

exercises.tip: "ما" plus "بـ" is the everyday way to negate a present verb.

exercises.prompt: Translate: 'OK, that works.'

too_formal.feedback: Correct but stiff; "تمام" and "ماشي" are what is said.

exercises.tip: "ماشي" literally means 'going', and is used for 'fine by me'.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means 'I agree' said by a woman?

too_formal.feedback: A formal written construction, not spoken.

exercises.tip: The ending "ـة" marks the feminine.

exercises.prompt: "هيدا مش صحيح" means:

too_formal.feedback: The formal way to say it; spoken Lebanese uses "مش" for not.

exercises.tip: "مش" is the everyday word for 'not' before a noun or adjective.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: 'حق / معك'.

too_formal.feedback: Formal phrasing, not the short spoken set phrase.

exercises.tip: "معك" literally means 'with you', so the phrase is 'right is with you'.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: 'الجديد / عالمطعم / منروح / برأيي'.

too_formal.item: في رأيي علينا الذهاب إلى المطعم الجديد
too_formal.feedback: Formal word order and vocabulary, not the spoken sentence.

exercises.tip: "برأيي" can open the sentence or close it.

phrases.arabic: لو كنت مكانك كنت عملت هيك

dialogue.speaker: Nadine
dialogue.arabic: شو فيكي يا سلمى؟ وجك أصفر
dialogue.english: What's wrong, Salma? Your face is pale.

dialogue.speaker: Salma
dialogue.english: I've had a headache for two days.

dialogue.speaker: Nadine
dialogue.english: It's better you go to the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Salma
dialogue.english: I don't want to, it scares me.

dialogue.speaker: Nadine
dialogue.english: I advise you not to wait long.

dialogue.speaker: Salma
dialogue.english: OK, what do you advise me now?

dialogue.speaker: Nadine
dialogue.transliteration: jarrbi had dawa w rtaa7i shwayy
dialogue.english: Try this medicine and rest a little.

dialogue.speaker: Salma
dialogue.english: It won't hurt me if I try it.

dialogue.speaker: Nadine
dialogue.transliteration: w khalliki haadye w ma testa3jeli
dialogue.english: And stay calm and don't rush.

dialogue.speaker: Salma
dialogue.english: You're right, thanks for the advice.

dialogue.speaker: Nadine
dialogue.english: Take care of yourself.

pair.english: What do you advise me to do?
Do I have to go to the doctor?

response.english: It won't hurt you to try.

pair.english: What would you do if you were me?

lessons.culture: In Lebanon advice tends to come unasked, especially from mothers, aunts and neighbours, and it is warm rather than pushy. The polite reply is "معك حق" or "إن شاء الله", even if you have no plan to follow it.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: 'شو بتنصحني إعمل؟'. Give a natural reply.

too_formal.item: أنصحك بأن تأخذ قسطا من الراحة
too_formal.feedback: Correct but bookish; "لازم تاخد" is how advice is really given.

exercises.tip: "لازم" plus a verb is the everyday 'you should'.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: 'لازم روح عالدكتور؟'. Give a natural reply saying yes.

too_formal.feedback: "نعم" and "الأفضل" are formal; spoken Lebanese says "إيه" and "الأحسن".

exercises.tip: "إيه" is yes in everyday speech.

exercises.prompt: Complete: '___ تاخد قسط راحة.' Meaning: You should get some rest. (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: "يجب أن" is formal; "لازم" is the spoken word.

exercises.tip: "لازم" is followed directly by the verb, with no "أن".

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'خليك ___ وما تستعجل.' Meaning: Stay calm and don't rush.

too_formal.feedback: "هادئا" is the formal spelling; "هادي" is what is said.

exercises.tip: "هادي" for a man, "هادية" for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Translate: 'It's better you go to the doctor.'

too_formal.item: من الأفضل أن تذهب إلى الطبيب
too_formal.feedback: Written-style; spoken Lebanese says "الأحسن" and "دكتور".

exercises.tip: "عالدكتور" is "على الدكتور" run together; "ذهب" becomes "راح" in speech.

exercises.prompt: Translate: 'I advise you not to do this.'

too_formal.feedback: Formal written Arabic; spoken Lebanese says "ما تعمل هيك".

exercises.tip: "ما تعمل" after "بنصحك" means 'not to do'.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means 'Take care of yourself' to a man?

too_formal.feedback: Correct but formal; "دير بالك عحالك" is the warm spoken one.

exercises.tip: "دير بالك" literally means 'turn your mind', used for 'be careful'.

exercises.prompt: "لو كنت مكانك كنت عملت هيك" means:
exercises.answer: If I were you, I'd do this
accepted: If I were you, I'd do this
If I were you I would do this

too_formal.feedback: The written form; spoken Lebanese says "كنت عملت" instead of "لفعلت".

exercises.tip: "مكانك" means 'your place'.
options: If I were you, I'd do this
It won't hurt you to try

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: 'راحة / قسط / تاخد / لازم'.

too_formal.item: يجب عليك أن تأخذ قسطا من الراحة
too_formal.feedback: Formal register; "لازم" starts the spoken sentence.

exercises.tip: "لازم" comes first, then the verb, then what to take.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: 'تستعجل / وما / هادي / خليك'.

too_formal.feedback: Formal imperative; spoken Lebanese uses "خليك" and "ما".

exercises.tip: "خليك" plus an adjective means 'stay ...'.

phrases.arabic: الأكل بارد شوي، ممكن تسخنلي ياه؟
phrases.transliteration: el 2akel baared shwayy, mumken tsakhkhenli yaah?

phrases.arabic: مش قصدي ضايقك، بس هيدا مهم
هيدا مش متل اللي شفتو بالصورة
phrases.transliteration: hayda mish metl elli shifto bes suura

phrases.arabic: ما في مشكلة، بس بدي وضح شي
phrases.transliteration: ma fii mishkle, bass badde waddi7 shi

dialogue.speaker: Zeina
dialogue.english: Excuse me, there's a small problem.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Welcome, what's the problem?

dialogue.speaker: Zeina
dialogue.arabic: آسفة عالإزعاج، بس هيدا مش اللي طلبتو
dialogue.english: Sorry to bother you, but this isn't what I ordered.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Forgive me, I'll change it now.

dialogue.speaker: Zeina
dialogue.english: And also the food is a bit cold.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: I'll heat it up for you right away.

dialogue.speaker: Zeina
dialogue.english: The order was very late too.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: You're right, I'm very sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Zeina
dialogue.arabic: ما في مشكلة، بس بدي وضح شي
dialogue.transliteration: ma fii mishkle, bass badde waddi7 shi
dialogue.english: No problem, but I'd like to clarify something.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Of course, go ahead.

dialogue.speaker: Zeina
dialogue.english: Thanks, well done.

response.english: There's a mistake in the bill.

pair.english: Do you want your money back?

response.english: No, I just want to change it.
A bit cold, can you heat it up?

lessons.culture: Lebanese soften a complaint with "لو سمحت" or "آسف عالإزعاج" before naming the problem, and often end with "يعطيك العافية" so it never feels like an attack on the person. In restaurants people often switch to a bit of French or English, like "merci" or "sorry", to keep the tone light.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: 'شو المشكلة؟'. Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but written; spoken Lebanese says "في غلط بالحساب".

exercises.tip: "في" is 'there is', and "الحساب" is the everyday word for the bill.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: 'بدك يرجعولك المصاري؟'. Give a natural reply saying no.

too_formal.feedback: Formal register; "بدي" is the spoken 'I want'.

exercises.tip: "بدي" plus a verb or object means 'I want'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: '___ سمحت، في مشكلة صغيرة.' Meaning: Excuse me, there's a small problem.

too_formal.feedback: "من فضلك" is correct but formal; "لو سمحت" is the everyday opener.

exercises.tip: "لو سمحت" literally means 'if you allow'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'هيدا ___ اللي طلبتو.' Meaning: This isn't what I ordered.

too_formal.feedback: "ليس" is formal; "مش" is the spoken 'not'.

exercises.tip: "مش" negates a noun or adjective; "ما" negates a verb.

exercises.prompt: Translate: 'There's a mistake in the bill.'

too_formal.feedback: Formal written Arabic; the spoken form uses "في" and "غلط".

exercises.tip: "بالحساب" is "بـ" plus "الحساب" run together.

exercises.prompt: Translate: 'Can you help me with this matter?'

too_formal.item: هل تستطيع مساعدتي في هذا الموضوع؟
too_formal.feedback: Correct but formal; "فيك" is the everyday 'can you'.

exercises.tip: "فيك" is the common Lebanese 'are you able to'.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase politely opens a complaint?

too_formal.feedback: "شكوى رسمية" sounds like a formal written complaint, not a polite spoken one.

exercises.tip: Start soft with "لو سمحت", then name the problem.

exercises.prompt: "يعطيك العافية" is best used to mean:

too_formal.feedback: Very formal; "يعطيك العافية" is warmer and everyday.

exercises.tip: It is said to anyone who has worked or helped, and is answered with "الله يعافيك".

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: 'صغيرة / مشكلة / في / سمحت / لو'.

too_formal.feedback: Formal wording, not the spoken opener.

exercises.tip: The polite opener comes first, then the problem.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: 'بالحساب / غلط / في'.

too_formal.feedback: Formal wording, not how it is said aloud.

exercises.tip: "في" comes first, like 'there is'.

challenge.title: How Was Your Week?
challenge.instructions: Write a short conversation between two friends who run into each other. One asks how the other is feeling, hears about a problem, gives some advice, and the other politely raises one more small complaint before agreeing on what to do.
required_elements: a question asking how someone feels, using "كيفك" or "كيفِك"
at least one feeling word such as "تعبان", "مبسوط" or "قلقان"
a piece of advice using "لازم" or "الأحسن"
agreement or disagreement using "معك حق" or "ما بوافقك"
a polite complaint opened with "لو سمحت" or "آسف عالإزعاج"

dialogue.speaker: Hala
dialogue.english: How are you today?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.arabic: أنا شوي قلقان، عندي كتير شغل
dialogue.english: I'm a little worried, I have a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Hala
dialogue.arabic: الأحسن تاخد قسط راحة قبل ما تتعب أكتر
dialogue.transliteration: el a7san taakhod 2ost raa7a 2abl ma tit3ab aktar
dialogue.english: It's better you get some rest before you get more tired.

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.arabic: معِك حق. آسف عالإزعاج، بس القهوة تأخرت كتير
dialogue.english: You're right. Sorry to bother you, but the coffee is very late.

dialogue.speaker: Hala
dialogue.english: Don't worry, we'll ask now.

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.english: OK, thanks for the advice.
